Q: Avoid overwriting existing columns in data.table functions A:

I can offer an update to this solution, building on what has been said and taking advantage of the data.table env argument. I start with a function that ensures unique column names only, using snippets from the earlier answers.

library(data.table)

# function to edit new names to prevent overwriting
edit_col_names <- function(DT, proposed_new_names) {
    
    # existing column names
    exist_names <- colnames(DT)
    
    # edit new names (if needed) to distinguish from existing names
    uniq_names <- make.unique(c(exist_names, proposed_new_names))
    
    # return the edited new names
    new_names <- setdiff(uniq_names, exist_names)[]
}

Next I setup the working data frame similar to the one in the examples above.

# setup the data frame
DT <- as.data.table(mtcars)[1:10, .(mpg)]
DT[, ':=' (
    q = mpg, 
    q.1 = 2 * mpg
)]

Define the names of the two new columns and the functions that will create them. I purposefully define one column z that does not match existing column names and one q that does. Again, I encode the same expressions as those in the previous example.

# names of the new columns to be added to data frame
new_cols <- c("z", "q")

# functions that define the new columns
f1 <- function(x) {z <- 3 * x}
f2 <- function(x) {q <- f1(x) + 4}

To start the work, edit the proposed column names to prevent overwriting.

# edit new names to prevent overwriting
revised_new_cols <- edit_col_names(y, new_cols)

Lastly, use the env argument to bring all the pieces together. Character strings of the new column names and the function names are passed to the NSE expressions via the symbols written in uppercase. Uppercase is not a requirement, but it is a handy convention for keeping track of the substitutions.

DT[, ':=' (Z = F1(mpg), 
           Q = F2(mpg)), 
  env = list(Z = revised_new_cols[1], 
             Q = revised_new_cols[2],
             F1 = "f1", 
             F2 = "f2")]

The result DT matches the result x in the previous answer.

To see the substitutions, we can use the verbose argument.

# view the 'j' argument after substitution
DT[, ':=' (Z = F1(mpg), 
           Q = F2(mpg)), 
  env = list(Z = revised_new_cols[1], 
             Q = revised_new_cols[2],
             F1 = "f1", 
             F2 = "f2"), 
  verbose = TRUE]

For details on the env argument, see the vignette Programming on data.table.

Q: in std::valarray, how to access to elements from the end indexes (in a direct way): the last element, the second-to-last element, etc A:

// error: 'class std::valarray<int>' has no member named 'end'

std::valarray is not a container. You can use std::end(va).

Q: Invalidate strings that contain building/home number (18, 18a, 18b) A:

Add a dot at your expression :

^[\p{L}\d. ]+(?!\d).$

Otherwise the test is not done.

Q: Redirect stderr to both stderr and stdout A:

What do you need separate stderr output for?

Because a log of errors without the (audit) log of actions that led to the error is, generally, unhelpful. Unless the error message includes the complete call-chain with function arguments and/or more details, which is never the case -- in good software designs callees have no information about their callers (e.g. strlen).

Normally, it is desirable to also write both stdout and stderr outputs into one log file, in addition to writing these into the one same pseudoterminal multiplexer device. The latter means that redirecting stderr into stdout (or vice versa) keeps writes in the same order into the same pseudoterminal multiplexer device. (The order of outputs of multiple threads writing into stdout and stderr simultaneously is always affected by these redirections.)

Hence:

my-cmd |& tee -i my-cmd.log

redirects both stderr and stdout writes into one pipe while keeping the original order of writes intact. tee writes these into one log file and into the same pseudoterminal multiplexer device. The terminal output is identical to that of plain my-cmd invocation with no redirections.

tee -i ignores signals, deferring signal handling to my-cmd. A prior set -o pipefail obviates having to examine PIPESTATUS.

Q: How can I pass the data type in a generic linked list to the GDB print command? A:

You can pass type name separately by executing custom command in GDB command line.

Let's start with the actual pretty printer:

class ListPrinter:
    # NOTE: static variable which stores user-specified value type
    value_type = None

    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value

    def to_string(self):
        return 'List[%d]' % int(self.value['count'])

    def print_node_value(self, value):
        if int(value) == 0:
            return value
        vtype = ListPrinter.value_type
        if vtype is None:
            return value
        # here we cast to the desired type
        return value.cast(vtype.pointer()).dereference()

    def children(self):
        # this is generic function for pretty-printing linked lists
        return linked_list_children_list(
            # start node
            self.value['head'].dereference()['next'],
            # given a node, returns the next node
            lambda x: x.dereference()['next'],
            # given a node, returns the value of the node
            lambda x: self.print_node_value(x.dereference()['data'])
        )

The global variable ListPrinter.value_type specifies the type to the printer. We can set it using a custom command (I took the syntax from this answer):

# user command that it directly runnable from the GDB console
class SetListType(gdb.Command):
    def __init__(self):
        super(SetListType, self).__init__('set_list_type', gdb.COMMAND_USER)

    def invoke(self, argument, fromtty):
        argv = gdb.string_to_argv(argument)
        if len(argv) != 1:
            print('Pass one argument: name of the C++ type to be displayed inside List')
            return
        typename = argv[0]
        # find the type and set it into global variable
        vtype = gdb.lookup_type(typename)
        ListPrinter.value_type = vtype

SetListType()

Now connect the Python code to GDB, and try printing:

-exec print mylist
$1 = 0x5555555592a0 List[10] = {[0] = 0x5555555592f0, [1] = 0x555555559330, [2] = 0x555555559370, [3] = 0x5555555593b0, [4] = 0x5555555593f0, [5] = 0x555555559430, [6] = 0x555555559470, [7] = 0x5555555594b0, [8] = 0x5555555594f0, [9] = 0x555555559530}

Nothing interesting so far. Now let's set the type:

-exec set_list_type int

After that the printout gets better:

-exec print mylist
$2 = 0x5555555592a0 List[10] = {[0] = 0, [1] = 71, [2] = 42, [3] = 13, [4] = 84, [5] = 55, [6] = 26, [7] = 97, [8] = 68, [9] = 39}

Alternatives

However, I don't believe this approach is a good idea. It is nice for some simple toy examples, but not so good in a larger codebase. What if you have several lists of different types in your field of view? How is it going to work with IDEs? What if you have a list of entities, and every entity has a member being a list of integers... how are you going to inspect this?

If you were using C++, you could turn your xlist into a template class and thus embed the data type into the type of the list. In pure C, the only option is to save the data type inside the xlist structure.

One way to do it is to add a enum listing all the allowed data types. This should work, but feels a bit limiting. Instead, you can simply save your data type as a string.

First, let's update your C structure:

typedef struct xlist {
    ...
    int                   count;        /* number of nodes in list           */
    const char           *dataType;     /* string literal: type of node data */
} xlist;

Then, read and lookup the type inside pretty printer constructor:

class ListPrinter:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        try:
            typename = str(value['dataType'].string())
            self.value_type = gdb.lookup_type(typename)
        except:
            self.value_type = None

The conversion of node data stays mostly the same:

    def print_node_value(self, value):
        if int(value) == 0:
            return value
        vtype = self.value_type
        if vtype is None:
            return value
        # here we cast to the desired type
        return value.cast(vtype.pointer()).dereference()

This solution works the same, but does not require any special actions on GDB side. Just inspect your data in GDB or IDE as you like. Don't forget to assign proper string literal into dataType!
